Q: How can I create snippets like Emmet's in VS Code? A:

The easiest way is to use VS Code User Snippets. You can create your own short abbreviation that expands into a full block of code.

For example, if you often write a basic HTML card, you could create a snippet like this:

  1. In VS Code, press Ctrl + Shift + P.

  2. Search for “Snippets: Configure User Snippets”.

  3. Choose html.json (or create a language-specific snippet file).

  4. Add something like:

"Basic Card": {
    "prefix": "mycard",
    "body": [
        "<div class=\"card\">",
        "  <h2>$1</h2>",
        "  <p>$2</p>",
        "</div>"
    ],
    "description": "Creates a basic card"
}

  1. Save the file.

  2. Open an HTML file, type mycard, and press Tab.

VS Code will expand it into the complete HTML and let you jump between $1 and $2 with Tab.

Q: Why do we need the “finally:” clause in Python, if we can just write code after the “try:” block? A:

Here's a peice of code to clarify the difference:

def f(a, b):
    try:
        a / b
        print('In try block')

    except TypeError:
        print('In except block')

    finally:
        print('In finally block')

    print('Outside')

f(0, 1)

Output:

In try block 
In finally block 
Outside

(No errors, except block skipped.)

f(1, 0)

Output:

In finally block

Traceback (most recent call last):
a/b
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

(No exception handling is specified for ZeroDivisionError and only the finally block is executed.)

f(0, '1')

Output:

In except block 
In finally block 
Outside

(Exception is handled properly and the program is not interrupted.)

Note: If you have an except block to handle all types of errors, the finally block will be superfluous.

Q: In an SSH configuration file, is there a way to split a "Host" directive over multiple lines? A:

In this scenario, do foo.com, bar.com, and bin.com all route to the same Hostname?

I guess it depends what you are looking for, though. This doesn't consolidate things in the way I think you are looking for, but here is one option that might work for you. You can use Host "aliases" to define the hosts and then reference them later in your config file.

For example:

Host h1
Hostname foo.com

Host h2
Hostname bar.com

Host k1
Hostname bin.com

Host other
Hostname other.net

Host h* k* other
Username baz
IdentityFile qux.txt

Q: Preflight CORS error followed by 404 error A:

The API which you call does not consider Authorization a CORS-allowed header:

Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, X-Requested-With

Therefore you cannot make requests from a different origin that include authorization like

auth: {
  username: "xyxyx",
  password: "xyxy"
}

because this leads to an Authorization header. This restriction can only be lifted by the one who wrote the API. It must be:

Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, X-Requested-With, Authorization

Q: How can I stop relying on AI when writing code? A:

This question is kinda... generic.

First of all, what code are your trying to write? Are you actually learning a programming language while building apps, building a framework for your job...

If you are trying to learn, simply "waste" your time trying to build something that actually compiles and then (and ONLY then) ask AI if your code is well written or not. Don't ask AI for tips, boilerplate code or anything else. Just make mistakes, fix them and spend bunch of hours on the same, simple problem until you get something working. I'm saying that because if you don't really struggle on things, you are never gonna improve. Using AI as an oracle is simply useless when you are trying to learn, it's like asking a senior developer to fix your code without actually learning how to write "senior developer" code.

If you are building apps for your job, it's actually a different topic. AI simply improves your efficiency, because you can build apps in just minutes without losing your mind in bad documented code. BUT in this case you're goal is not to "improve", instead you are trying to find a good solution for your needs... and it's not that bad. AI can build code which is efficient, scalable and even "secure", avoiding common mistakes that programmers do (ever heard of buffer overflow?). It's not a "he is a bad programmer" or "it's his fault", but it's kinda hard to create code and AI removes many layers of difficulty from this. In this case I think the best scenario is that AI generates code, you see that and try to figure out why it works, how it works and how you could improve that (syntatically, semantically...)

So the answer really depends on your needs. If you are trying to learn something, simply don't use that at all if you are always prompting "could you please give me a tip" or "how could I do that?", just cry on your keyboard trying to figure out how to fix a segmentation fault error. If you need a piece of code for your job, and the deadline is tomorrow, ask AI to generate that and figure out why he wrote that. Probably a lot of that code is simply boilerplate, but understand why he wrote that and how you could fix that or "Is this really what I would have written" and change that if you find that it is unclear (even renaming variables could save a life one day...)

Q: How can I restrict a method to only classes implementing a specific interface in Java? A:

What would be the idiomatic Java design for enforcing this restriction?

I don't know about idiomatic, but the way I would do this is to change the method signature from public void heal(int amount) to public void receiveHealing(Healer source).

Instead of accepting an integer, forcing the method to require a Healer object uses Java's type system to guarantee that a heal is impossible unless an actual Healer is present to initiate it.
